newsitem.title: USA: Clinton woos southern voters, Dole in California.
newsitem.headline: Clinton woos southern voters, Dole in California.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton wooed voters in the Republican stronghold of Virginia on Sunday as challenger Bob Dole extended his stay in California in a last-ditch bid to avert defeat on Nov. 5.
Clinton won key endorsements from the New York Times, the Boston Globe and the Philadelphia Inquirer this weekend, while Dole picked up the vote of New York Mayor Ralph Giuliani.

"Republicans complain that Clinton has stolen many of their programs and ideas, but what Clinton has really managed to steal is the broad center of the American political spectrum -- a position we hope he will keep during a second term," the Inquirer wrote in an editorial published on Sunday.
Dole mentioned the New York Times endorsement for Clinton in a California rally, saying "even they had to apologize for his ethics. Why apologize? Why not send him back to Little Rock, Arkansas?"

A buoyant Clinton, who has ignored Dole's broadsides, embarked on a three-day seven-state trip, starting with a rally in Virginia, a state that has not voted to put a Democrat in the White House since 1964 when it supported Lyndon Johnson.
Analysts and polls say Clinton may win Virginia and several other typically Republican states.
"Most people in Virginia have been voting against members of my party for president for over three decades now and I know how hard it is to break a habit," Clinton said.
"One of the things we all teach our kids is that some habits have to be broken," he said to laughter from the crowd.
Clinton also got some good news on the economic front, although it came from an unlikely source.
Congressional Republicans on Sunday said the U.S. budget deficit for the financial year that ended Sept. 30 will be about $109 billion, the lowest in a decade.

They claimed credit for the figure, which is still not official, releasing the data shortly after White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta hinted Clinton will have "some good news" on the U.S. budget deficit.

The Reuters daily tracking poll showed Clinton increasing his lead over Dole among likely voters to 13.4 percentage points. The CNN/USA Today Gallup poll showed Clinton leading by 20 points. ABC television had Clinton 15 points in front.
If that kind of lead held until Election Day Clinton would be in position to score a landslide of historic proportions.

Republican pollster Robert Teeter said it was unlikely that Dole would be able to pull ahead in the final days of a campaign where Clinton's lead has stayed remarkably stable for months. "There's no dynamic in this election," he said.
Clinton is seeking to buttress his commanding position in traditionally crucial Midwestern states like Illinois and Ohio, which he will visit on Monday and Tuesday.

He is also using the campaign's waning days to further objectives beyond his own re-election, like positioning Gore for a run at the White House in 2000, and helping Democrats regain control of Congress two years after Republicans took control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

"Everything I see gives me optimism that we will win both houses back. The Republicans botched a wonderful opportunity they had two years ago. They were radical. They were extreme," said Rep. Richard Gephardt of Missouri, who would become House Speaker if the Democrats took over.
But Republicans were still insisting that their polls showed they could still keep control of Congress.

Dole decided to stay an extra day in California, hoping to revive his challenge for the state's 54 Electoral College votes -- one fifth of the 270 needed to win the presidency in the U.S. indirect election system.

At a rally of Vietnamese-Americans in San Jose, Dole criticized Clinton for not doing enough to police the nation's borders and reiterated his support for a controversial ballot initiative to end affirmative action and preferences in government hiring, contracting and school admissions.

In recent days Dole's speeches have turned increasingly sour and abrasive. He not only attacked the media but even the public for failing to pay attention to what Dole believed were Clinton's serious ethical shortcomings.
White House adviser George Stephanopoulos, interviewed on NBC's "Meet the Press," said Clinton and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton had done nothing wrong.
"Bob Dole ought to apologize" for some of the claims he has made in recent days, Stephanopoulos said.
Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, stuck in single digits in the polls, maintained his own assault on Clinton's ethics in an interview on the same program.
"You should never let anyone be president of the United States who does not have a strong moral and ethical base," Perot said.
